lines: {target}? Bright trunks can make shadows easy to miss. I would stay close enough to hear the bell.
If anyone heads for Birch Forest, tell them. Don't let the pretty light lower your guard. I will be at the bell.
White bark shows marks, but not always danger. I'll remember that from near the bell.
Birch Forest is no small story. Running the wrong way is still running.
I will remember Birch Forest as a pale forest with quiet steps under it. I will stay where I can hear the bell.
I have packed for trips before. This time I would remember food, torches, and a compass. The spoon can stay home.
At Birch Forest, I would keep the slowest traveler beside me. There is a fair chance that traveler is me.
Pretty scenery will not stop me tripping over a hidden root.
If everyone went quiet near a spider, I would start walking the other way.
If someone needed help at Birch Forest, I would fetch help and point them toward the white trunks.
Keeping my socks dry in Birch Forest may be too much to ask.
Birch Forest would make me curious. I would be glad someone else knew when we had wandered far enough.
If the plan went wrong, I would head straight for the last open clearing.
Before wandering around Birch Forest, I would make sure the last open clearing was easy to find again.
At Birch Forest, fresh air would count as a landmark even when the map said otherwise.
Rain can change Birch Forest quickly, so I would keep one clear path home.
Seeing the pale trunks and thick grass would make our village paths seem wonderfully boring. I like boring paths.
A map of Birch Forest would help, especially with a large drawing of the last open clearing.
Extra torches are worth carrying when roots keep hiding in the grass.
The best part of Birch Forest could be telling the story from my own bed.
{target}? Pretty petals do not keep monsters away. I would stay close enough to hear the bell.
If anyone heads for Cherry Grove, tell them. Enjoy the flowers before dark, not after. I will be at the bell.
Pink leaves can make folk forget the sword at their side. I'll remember that from near the bell.
Cherry Grove is no small story. Running the wrong way is still running.
I will remember Cherry Grove as a beautiful hill that still needs torches. I will stay where I can hear the bell.
The trip home deserves daylight too, even if the interesting part used all of it.
I would warn the group about a bee near the blossoms, preferably before my voice became a squeak.
At Cherry Grove, I could spend too long staring at the pink trees across a gentle slope. Someone sensible should tug my sleeve.
At Cherry Grove, I would stay close enough to hear the group. I wander better than I return.
Before leaving for Cherry Grove, I would check twice that I had food, torches, and a compass. Then I would ask someone else.
A snack near the oldest cherry tree near the trail sounds like a good way to remember where it is.
I could use cherry wood to mark the route, provided it did not all look the same.
At Cherry Grove, I would place lights where they pointed home, not where they looked pretty.
At Cherry Grove, fresh air would count as a landmark even if the map disagreed.
I would forget one part of Cherry Grove and remember a completely useless pebble.
We should meet at the oldest cherry tree near the trail. Otherwise I might wait somewhere memorable only to me.
Someone should remind me that the oldest cherry tree near the trail is for getting home, not just admiring.
Rushing around the pink trees across a gentle slope would only help the trouble arrive sooner.
Strange places dislike idle hands. I can carry the food bag and keep mine busy.
If I took a wrong turn near the pink trees across a gentle slope, I would admit it before it became an expedition.
{target}? Thick leaves make noon feel late. I would stay close enough to hear the bell.
If anyone heads for Dark Forest, tell them. Place torches before you need them. I will be at the bell.
Mushrooms grow big where sunlight gives up. I'll remember that from near the bell.
Dark Forest is no small story. Running the wrong way is still running.
I will remember Dark Forest as a forest that keeps its own night. I will stay where I can hear the bell.
If I could still reach the last patch of open sky, I would call myself only partly lost. That is better than usual.
I wonder what Dark Forest smells like. This is not important, but my nose never asks permission.
If the light failed near the dark oak trees blocking the sky, I would not pretend my eyes had adjusted.
Someone should walk behind me at Dark Forest. I stop for interesting nonsense without warning.
I would remember Dark Forest because of branches creaking above the mushrooms. My ears keep better notes than I do.
Has anyone counted how many ways roots hidden in deep shadow can become a problem? I would stop at one.
I can imagine carrying traces of dark oak home from Dark Forest.
A shared meeting place is useful because yelling directions has never improved mine.
If someone needed help at Dark Forest, I would fetch the sensible people and remember where they went.
A heavy pack is poor company on the return from Dark Forest.
Bringing food, torches, and a compass sounds sensible for Dark Forest. I should write that down before I pack biscuits.
I would wonder how the dark oak trees blocking the sky came to be there, then remember I need not find out.
The village has fewer surprises than Dark Forest. This is one of its finest qualities.
At Dark Forest, I would point at suspicious things instead of picking them up. That is progress.
At Dark Forest, I could spend too long staring at the dark oak trees blocking the sky. Someone sensible should tug my sleeve.
{target}? Flowers make poor armor. I would stay close enough to hear the bell.
If anyone heads for Flower Forest, tell them. Enjoy daylight and leave before monsters admire it too. I will be at the bell.
Bees and blossoms do not stop arrows. I'll remember that from near the bell.
Flower Forest is no small story. Running the wrong way is still running.
I will remember Flower Forest as a soft-looking forest that still needs caution. I will stay where I can hear the bell.
At Flower Forest, I would keep the slowest traveler beside me. There is a fair chance that traveler is me.
I would bring news home if a bee guarding its nest blocked the route. Quickly and with many hand gestures.
At Flower Forest, nobody needs to prove bravery by ignoring a hole hidden by tall flowers. Danger does not award prizes.
I would wave at Flower Forest when leaving. I wave at places sometimes. They rarely wave back.
Seeing a bee guarding its nest would remind me of an urgent appointment somewhere behind me.
I might improve a story about Flower Forest, but I would keep the dangerous details honest.
I would remember Flower Forest because of bees moving among the flowers. My ears keep better notes than I do.
If I announced that I knew the way, someone should quietly check the widest patch of open flowers.
If I forgot why we stopped, I would not assume the reason had gone away.
At Flower Forest, even ordinary oak wood could hide an unexpected problem.
The first thing I would notice at Flower Forest is the flowers filling the spaces between trees. The second would be where I put my feet.
Before leaving for Flower Forest, I would check twice that I had food, torches, and a compass. Then I would ask someone else.
I would rather turn back early than discover the widest patch of open flowers was farther away than it looked.
I remember places by smells I cannot describe. Flower Forest sounds likely to become one.
Before wandering around Flower Forest, I would make sure the widest patch of open flowers was easy to find again.
{target}? Trees hide both roads and trouble. I would stay close enough to hear the bell.
If anyone heads for Forest, tell them. Keep the sun or a torch in mind. I'll be at the bell.
Leaves make every sound arrive late. I'll remember that from near the bell.
Forest is no small story. Running the wrong way is still running.
I will remember Forest as ordinary woods, which is how they fool people. I will stay where I can hear the bell.
I would count everyone before leaving the last open clearing. Somebody else should check my counting.
I might improve a story about Forest, but I would keep the dangerous details honest.
I have no clever trick for a spider between the trunks. Leaving is a trick I can usually manage.
At Forest, I would measure distance in snacks. Three snacks is not nearby.
Nothing found at Forest would be worth losing sight of the last open clearing.
On the way back from Forest, I would follow our marks instead of inventing a better route.
I would eat before reaching Forest. Hungry me makes decisions that ordinary me questions.
I would ask before moving anything at Forest. Then I would wait for the answer.
At Forest, the sound of branches creaking beyond sight could keep me awake. So could wondering whether it had stopped.
I have packed for trips before. This time I would remember food, torches, and a compass before a spoon.
I picture Forest and think of the trees beyond the path. Pictures leave out the dangerous walking.
I might be wrong about Forest. I would prefer to be wrong from a safe spot.
If Forest wanted me relaxed, it could move roots and low branches hiding the ground somewhere else.
I would rest before tired feet made roots and low branches hiding the ground harder to handle.
There is time to think twice about roots and low branches hiding the ground. If not, that is another reason to leave.
{target}? Old bright trees hide long shadows. I would stay close enough to hear the bell.
If anyone heads for Old Growth Birch Forest, tell them. Mark trunks and do not wander by moonlight. I will be at the bell.
Big birches make folk feel smaller than they expect. I'll remember that from near the bell.
Old Growth Birch Forest is no small story. Running the wrong way is still running.
I will remember Old Growth Birch Forest as pale old trees standing too quietly. I will stay where I can hear the bell.
If I took a wrong turn near the pale trunks and thick grass, I would admit it before it became an expedition.
Perhaps I am wrong about the pale trunks and thick grass. I am also perhaps excellent with directions.
At Old Growth Birch Forest, nobody needs to prove bravery by ignoring roots and low branches hiding the ground. Danger does not award prizes.
If I noticed a spider between the trunks, I would give it all the room it wanted and perhaps extra.
I would ask what rain under the leaves meant for the trip. Guessing at conditions has gone badly before.
I would rather turn back early than discover the last open clearing was farther away than it looked.
I have packed for trips before. This time I would remember food, torches, and a compass before a spoon.
The useful story is the one that helps the next traveler find the last open clearing.
Shadows around birch bark could make a poor shortcut look convincing.
My feet should vote before I walk through the pale trunks and thick grass. They usually vote for home.
I wonder whether branches creaking beyond sight would seem louder when everyone stopped talking. I am rarely first to stop.
For Old Growth Birch Forest, I would set out early enough to return while the bell still sounded ordinary.
Old Growth Birch Forest would make me curious. It would also make me glad someone else knows when to stop.
My eyes would go straight to the pale trunks and thick grass at Old Growth Birch Forest. Someone else should watch the path.
Before wandering around Old Growth Birch Forest, I would make sure the last open clearing was easy to find again.
{target}? Old pines make deep shadows. I would stay close enough to hear the bell.
If anyone heads for Old Growth Pine Taiga, tell them. Follow torchlight and watch for wolves. I will be at the bell.
The trunks rise like walls without doors. I'll remember that from near the bell.
Old Growth Pine Taiga is no small story. Running the wrong way is still running.
I will remember Old Growth Pine Taiga as cold old trees with a long memory. I will stay where I can hear the bell.
I picture Old Growth Pine Taiga and think of the spruce trees and berry bushes. Pictures leave out the dangerous walking.
If the map and the last open clearing disagreed, I would listen to the landmark.
At Old Growth Pine Taiga, I would listen when someone said I was going the wrong way. Eventually.
I would leave Old Growth Pine Taiga before dark made the spruce trees and berry bushes harder to read.
A heavy pack is poor company on the return from Old Growth Pine Taiga.
I would look closely at spruce needles without picking up anything I did not understand. Experience taught me that.
I would remember Old Growth Pine Taiga because of branches creaking beyond sight. My ears keep better notes than I do.
At Old Growth Pine Taiga, I would tie everything twice. Loose laces have excellent timing.
At Old Growth Pine Taiga, fresh air would count as a landmark even if the map disagreed.
I would forget one part of Old Growth Pine Taiga and remember a completely useless pebble.
If I noticed a spider between the trunks, I would give it all the room it wanted and perhaps extra.
Before exploring the spruce trees and berry bushes, I would make everyone agree to meet at the last open clearing.
Rushing around the spruce trees and berry bushes would only help the trouble arrive sooner.
Dealing with roots and low branches hiding the ground would be enough to change my plan for Old Growth Pine Taiga. My plans are not precious.
At Old Growth Pine Taiga, I would place lights where they pointed home, not where they looked pretty.
{target}? Spruce shade keeps danger close. I would stay close enough to hear the bell.
If anyone heads for Old Growth Spruce Taiga, tell them. Move slow and keep the path marked. I will be at the bell.
Moss and roots make quiet footing treacherous. I'll remember that from near the bell.
Old Growth Spruce Taiga is no small story. Running the wrong way is still running.
I will remember Old Growth Spruce Taiga as old spruce country where paths vanish fast. I will stay where I can hear the bell.
I would not trade the last loaf for a souvenir from Old Growth Spruce Taiga. Please remind me I said that.
I would not decide that branches creaking beyond sight meant no trouble at Old Growth Spruce Taiga without asking someone else.
I would probably spend too long looking at spruce needles at Old Growth Spruce Taiga. Everything interesting slows me down.
I know the sound people make when I miss a sign. I hope not to hear it while dealing with roots and low branches hiding the ground.
I would point at the last open clearing three times and still ask whether everyone saw it.
If I stumbled around spruce needles, I would check my boots before blaming the ground.
At Old Growth Spruce Taiga, patience could be the cleverest thing I managed all day.
At Old Growth Spruce Taiga, even village chores sound good. None of them involve roots and low branches hiding the ground.
I would forget one part of Old Growth Spruce Taiga and remember a completely useless pebble.
If someone needed help at Old Growth Spruce Taiga, I would fetch the sensible people and remember where they went.
After Old Growth Spruce Taiga, resting on the way home counts too. Stories make home feel closer than it is.
Bringing food, torches, and a compass sounds sensible for Old Growth Spruce Taiga. I should write that down before I pack biscuits.
I have no clever trick for a spider between the trunks. Leaving is a trick I can usually manage.
If rain under the leaves made Old Growth Spruce Taiga harder to read, I would head back while I could call it my idea.
I would know I reached Old Growth Spruce Taiga when the spruce trees and berry bushes made me forget what I meant to say.
{target}? Cold trees make every path look alike. I would stay close enough to hear the bell.
If anyone heads for Taiga, tell them. Mark the way and listen for wolves. I'll be at the bell.
Spruce needles keep secrets on the ground. I'll remember that from near the bell.
Taiga is no small story. Running the wrong way is still running.
I will remember Taiga as cold woods where a bell would sound small. I will stay where I can hear the bell.
Taiga would make me curious. It would also make me glad someone else knows when to stop.
Dealing with roots and low branches hiding the ground would be enough to change my plan for Taiga. My plans are not precious.
If rain under the leaves made Taiga harder to read, I would head back while I could call it my idea.
I might be wrong about Taiga. I would prefer to be wrong from a safe spot.
If I could still reach the last open clearing, I would call myself only partly lost. That is better than usual.
Does Taiga make the spruce trees and berry bushes look stranger up close, or does that only happen to me?
I may not lead a rescue well at Taiga, but I can run home and ring the bell with real commitment.
If anyone got separated at Taiga, I would stay near the last open clearing and not improve the plan.
I have packed for trips before. This time I would remember food, torches, and a compass before a spoon.
A good memory of Taiga weighs less than a full pack and cannot fall on my foot.
At Taiga, even village chores sound good. None of them involve roots and low branches hiding the ground.
At Taiga, I would not walk closer to a spider between the trunks just because everyone went quiet.
I would rest before tired feet made roots and low branches hiding the ground harder to handle.
Stories never mention branches creaking beyond sight in enough detail. They leave out useful things like that.
Good light might help me avoid roots and low branches hiding the ground. That is worth the extra torches.
{target}? Hard wind makes trees and cliffs argue. I would stay close enough to hear the bell.
If anyone heads for Windswept Forest, tell them. Watch branches, slopes, and sudden drops. I will be at the bell.
The forest leans like it is bracing itself. I'll remember that from near the bell.
Windswept Forest is no small story. Running the wrong way is still running.
I will remember Windswept Forest as trees holding on to rough ground. I will stay where I can hear the bell.
I know the sound people make when I miss a sign. I hope not to hear it while dealing with loose ground near a wooded drop.
A snack near the lower clearing out of the wind sounds like a good way to remember where it is.
I have no clever trick for a spider between the leaning trunks. Leaving is a trick I can usually manage.
If I announced that I knew the way, someone should quietly check the lower clearing out of the wind.
I would know I reached Windswept Forest when the trees clinging to steep hills made me forget what I meant to say.
I would forget one part of Windswept Forest and remember a completely useless pebble.
I would bring a map to Windswept Forest, though somebody else should hold it the right way up.
I am poor at judging distance, especially when something interesting is at the other end.
After Windswept Forest, the village bell would sound better than any heroic song.
I remember places by smells I cannot describe. Windswept Forest sounds likely to become one.
At Windswept Forest, if carrying loot made it harder to deal with loose ground near a wooded drop, I would leave the loot. I hope.
I can imagine carrying traces of oak wood home from Windswept Forest.
A shared meeting place is useful because yelling directions has never improved mine.
At Windswept Forest, I would keep my hands off anything that clicked, hissed, glowed, or looked offended.
Curiosity could pull me toward the trees clinging to steep hills. A sensible hand on my shoulder could pull harder.
